entries.question: Who was Abijam's mother?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 15:2 names Abijam's mother as Maachah, daughter of Abishalom. 2 Chronicles 13:2 names her Michaiah, daughter of Uriel. The same king's mother is given two different names and two different fathers.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 15:2 — "his mother's name was Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom." 2 Chronicles 13:2 — "his mother's name also was Michaiah the daughter of Uriel." Different name. Different father. Same king.

Apologists work three angles. First, the name-variation move: Maachah and Michaiah may be two forms of the same name, or one of them is a nickname. The Hebrew forms *Ma'akah* and *Mikhayahu* are not phonologically related and have different theophoric structures — *Mikhayahu* contains the divine name Yah, *Ma'akah* does not. This is not a spelling variant. So the name-variant harmonization is weak.

Second, the family-genealogy move from Keil-Delitzsch and Archer: Maachah is identified in 2 Chronicles 11:20-22 as Rehoboam's wife and the daughter of Absalom (i.e., David's son). The proposal is that Maachah was actually the *granddaughter* of Absalom through his daughter Tamar, who married Uriel of Gibeah. So her father was Uriel, her grandfather was Abishalom (= Absalom), and she went by two names — Maachah (matching her grandmother Maacah, Absalom's mother per 2 Samuel 3:3) and Michaiah. This is a real attempt to reconcile the genealogies, and it does have some textual support in Josephus, *Antiquities* 8.249-250, which reads Tamar as the daughter of Absalom who married Uriel.

But the harmonization stacks multiple unstated assumptions: that Maachah went by two unrelated names, that "daughter of Abishalom" really means "granddaughter," and that an otherwise unattested marriage between Tamar and Uriel is the missing link. Critical scholars including Japhet (OTL, pp. 690-691) note that "daughter of" can sometimes mean "granddaughter" in Hebrew genealogies, but the more direct reading is that the Chronicler is working with a slightly different tradition or correcting Kings.

McKenzie in his AOTC volume on Chronicles notes that the Chronicler frequently adjusts genealogical and onomastic details from Kings, and the Maachah/Michaiah variation is likely one more instance. Verdict: the harmonization is possible but requires several silent assumptions to land. The texts as written disagree.

answers.answer_explanation:
Now in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam the son of Nebat reigned Abijam over Judah. 
			        Three years reigned he in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Maachah, the daughter of 
			        Abishalom. 1 Kings 15:1-2

Now in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam began Abijah to reign over
			    Judah. Three years reigned he in Jerusalem. His mother's 
			    name also was Michaiah the daughter of Uriel. 2 Chronicles 13:1-2

commentary_out.commentary:
1 Kings 15:2 names Abijam's mother "Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom," while 2 Chronicles 13:2 names her "Michaiah the daughter of Uriel." Same king, different maternal name, different maternal grandfather. Both elements of the genealogy diverge.

The first harmonizing instinct — that Maachah and Michaiah are variant spellings of one name — does not survive scrutiny of the Hebrew. *Ma'akah* (מַעֲכָה) and *Mikhayahu* (מִיכָיָהוּ, the form in the MT of 2 Chr 13:2) are not phonologically related and are differently constructed. *Mikhayahu* is a theophoric name built on the divine element Yah(u), meaning roughly "Who is like Yah?"; *Ma'akah* contains no theophoric element and derives from a different root. This is not the kind of orthographic variation seen with, say, Jehoiachin/Jeconiah/Coniah. So the simple name-variant solution is weak. (It is worth noting that the LXX of 2 Chronicles reads *Maacha*, harmonizing toward Kings — itself a sign that ancient copyists already felt the discrepancy and smoothed it.)

The more substantial harmonization, advanced by Keil-Delitzsch and Archer, reconstructs the family tree. 2 Chronicles 11:20-22 makes Maachah the favored wife of Rehoboam and "daughter of Absalom." The proposal is that Maachah was strictly the *granddaughter* of Absalom: Absalom's daughter Tamar (2 Sam 14:27) married Uriel of Gibeah, and their daughter was Maachah/Michaiah. On this reconstruction Uriel is her biological father (matching 2 Chr 13:2), Abishalom/Absalom her grandfather (matching the looser "daughter of" in 1 Kgs 15:2 and 2 Chr 11:20), and she carried two names. The appeal to "daughter of" meaning "granddaughter" is linguistically defensible — Hebrew *bat* and *ben* can skip generations, as with Laban called "son of Nahor" (Gen 29:5) when he was actually Nahor's grandson via Bethuel.

What must be stated plainly is that no ancient source actually attests the Tamar-Uriel marriage. It is a modern harmonizing inference, built by stitching together 2 Samuel 14:27 (Absalom had a daughter named Tamar) and 2 Chronicles 13:2 (Uriel of Gibeah), with the marriage between them supplied to bridge the gap. Josephus does not record it — *Antiquities* 8.249-250 discusses Abijah's reign and Absalom's line but transmits no Tamar-Uriel-Maachah link, so it cannot be cited as ancient corroboration. That is the soft underbelly of the reconstruction: the very datum that makes it work, the marriage, exists nowhere in the textual record.

What keeps this from being decisive is the stack of independent assumptions it requires to be true simultaneously: that one woman bore two etymologically unrelated names, that "daughter of Abishalom" silently means granddaughter in two separate books, and that the otherwise unattested Tamar-Uriel marriage is historical rather than a later inference manufactured to dissolve exactly this tension. Sara Japhet (OTL) acknowledges the granddaughter reading as grammatically available but judges the more economical explanation to be that the Chronicler worked from, or generated, a divergent genealogical tradition. Steven McKenzie documents the Chronicler's broader habit of adjusting names and genealogical details inherited from Kings, of which the Maachah/Michaiah divergence is plausibly one more instance. Verdict: harmonizable in principle through the granddaughter reconstruction (which has real grammatical and Josephan support), but the reconciliation purchases coherence with several unverifiable premises; as written the two texts disagree on both the name and the father.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The conflict can be reconciled if 'daughter of Abishalom' (1 Kgs 15:2) is read as 'granddaughter' — a documented Hebrew usage — with Uriel of Gibeah (2 Chr 13:2) as her actual father by Absalom's daughter Tamar, and Maachah/Michaiah as two names for the same woman. But this granddaughter bridge is a modern harmonizing reconstruction (Keil-Delitzsch, Archer) resting only on 2 Sam 14:27 plus 2 Chr 13:2; no ancient source attests the Tamar-Uriel marriage it requires. With the name pair also not a spelling variant, the reconciliation is grammatically possible but evidentially unsecured rather than proven.

entries.question: When did Baasha die?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 16:6-8 says Baasha died and his son Elah began to reign in the 26th year of Asa, putting Baasha's death no later than Asa's 26th year. 2 Chronicles 16:1 says Baasha came up against Judah and fortified Ramah in the 36th year of Asa — ten years after his death according to Kings. The Chronicler places a living, militarily active Baasha a decade after Kings says he was already dead.
entries.commentary:
The chronology in Kings is internally tight. Baasha reigned 24 years (1 Kings 15:33) starting in Asa's 3rd year, putting his death in Asa's 26th-27th year. 1 Kings 16:8 confirms Elah his son began to reign in Asa's 26th year. So Baasha is dead by Asa's 26th year, full stop.

Then 2 Chronicles 16:1 drops the bomb: "In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah, and built Ramah." Ten years after Kings says Baasha was dead and buried, Chronicles has him leading military campaigns.

The apologetic standard response, going back to Keil-Delitzsch and championed by Edwin Thiele in *The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings*, is that 2 Chronicles 16:1's "36th year of Asa" is not really year 36 of Asa's personal reign but year 36 of the *divided kingdom* (counting from the schism after Solomon's death). Under that interpretation, the divided-kingdom 36th year corresponds to Asa's actual 16th year, and Baasha is still alive. Thiele's scheme is the most popular resolution and has been adopted by Dillard (WBC 15, pp. 122-126) and Selman (TOTC).

Thiele's reading has two real problems. First, it requires a counting convention that the Chronicler does not signal anywhere in the text — "36th year of Asa" is the natural reading, and importing a divided-kingdom dating system to fix the contradiction is the textbook ad-hoc move. Second, Japhet (OTL, pp. 731-735) notes that the Chronicler everywhere else dates by individual royal years, never by divided-kingdom era; making this one verse the exception is special pleading. Third, even if you grant Thiele's scheme, you've conceded that the text as written produces a contradiction and needs an external chronological key to dissolve it.

The critical reading, advanced by Klein (Hermeneia), is that the Chronicler is reorganizing the sequence of Asa's reign to fit the theological scheme where Asa's earlier piety (chapters 14-15) is rewarded with peace and his later faithlessness (chapter 16) is punished with war. The chronological dislocation is theological framing, not a coded reference to divided-kingdom dating. Take your pick: Thiele's hidden calendar trick, or the Chronicler reshaping the chronology for theology. Either way, the surface reading is a contradiction.

answers.answer: In the 26th year of King Asa's reign.
answers.answer_explanation:
So Baasha slept with his fathers, and was buried in Tirzah: and Elah his son reigned in his stead.... 
				        In the twenty and sixth year of Asa king of Judah began Elah the son of Baasha to reign over Israel in Tirzah, two years. 
				        1 Kings 16:6-8

answers.answer: Sometime after the 36th year of King Asa's reign.
answers.answer_explanation:
In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah, and built Ramah. 
				        2 Chronicles 16:1

commentary_out.commentary:
The chronology in Kings is internally tight and self-consistent. Baasha reigned twenty-four years (1 Kings 15:33), beginning in Asa's third year. Simple arithmetic puts the end of his reign in Asa's twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh year, and 1 Kings 16:8 confirms it: "In the twenty and sixth year of Asa king of Judah began Elah the son of Baasha to reign over Israel in Tirzah." By the close of Asa's twenty-sixth year, then, Baasha is dead, his son Elah is on the throne, and within two more years Zimri has murdered Elah and Omri has seized power (1 Kings 16:9-22). The whole Baasha-Elah-Zimri-Omri sequence is compressed into Asa's late twenties.

Against this, 2 Chronicles 16:1 reads: "In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah, and built Ramah." A full decade after Kings has Baasha buried and his dynasty extinguished, Chronicles has him alive, mustering an army, and fortifying a border town against Judah. The figures cannot both be right on their face.

Two distinct harmonizations are on offer, and it is worth keeping them apart because they are routinely conflated. The first is the copyist-error reading, held by Keil and Delitzsch (and popularized in handbooks like Geisler-Howe): the two figures at issue — 2 Chronicles 15:19, which reports that there was no more war "until the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Asa," and 16:1, which dates the Baasha campaign to the "thirty-sixth" — are scribal corruptions of an original "fifteenth" and "sixteenth," so the campaign really falls in Asa's sixteenth year. The second is the divided-kingdom reading, favored by Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and endorsed by Edwin Thiele in *The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings* (p. 59): the figures are not regnal years of Asa at all but years reckoned from the division of the kingdom after Solomon's death, which again lands the event in Asa's actual sixteenth year, comfortably within Baasha's lifetime. The two routes reach the same date by opposite means — one by emending the number, the other by reinterpreting what the number counts. The divided-kingdom version has been adopted by Dillard (WBC 15, pp. 122-126) and Selman (TOTC) and, with Thiele's backing, remains the standard conservative answer; it is worth noting that even Archer faults it for lacking any parallel where the Chronicler dates by the schism era.

Three objections weigh against the divided-kingdom reading in particular. First, the convention is invisible in the text: "thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa" is unambiguous Hebrew, and reading it as a schism-era date requires importing a counting system the Chronicler nowhere announces. Second, as Japhet observes (OTL, pp. 731-735), the Chronicler dates consistently by individual regnal years everywhere else; making these two verses the lone exceptions is special pleading driven by the need to remove the discrepancy. Third, even granting Thiele's calendar, the concession is fatal to the harmonizer's larger claim: the text as transmitted yields a contradiction that only an external, unstated chronological key can dissolve.

The critical alternative, advanced by Klein (Hermeneia, pp. 232-237), reads the displacement as redactional and theological rather than calendrical. The Chronicler reorganized Asa's reign around a retribution scheme: early piety (2 Chr 14-15) earns rest and victory, later faithlessness (2 Chr 16) brings war, disease, and rebuke. The Baasha campaign is relocated into Asa's thirty-sixth year not because of a hidden era-count but because the Chronicler needed Asa's reliance on Ben-Hadad of Aram, and his rebuke by the seer Hanani, to fall in the period of decline. The numbers serve the moral architecture of the narrative. On this view the figure is the Chronicler's own construction, not a scribal corruption of a schism-era source.

A further wrinkle favors the critical reading: the underlying problem is not merely a copied number but the placement of an entire episode that Kings situates a decade earlier (1 Kings 15:16-22 sets the Ramah affair in the ongoing Asa-Baasha hostilities, with no thirty-sixth-year notice). The Chronicler has both relocated the event and supplied a date incompatible with his own source. Whether one attributes the result to a misread era-heading or to deliberate theological reshaping, the surface text presents a dead king conducting a war. Verdict: genuine contradiction in the received text, resolvable only by positing either an unsignaled dating convention (Thiele) or theological redaction of the chronology (Klein/Japhet) — both of which concede the plain reading conflicts.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Two distinct conservative routes reach Asa's 16th year, while Baasha still lived: (1) the copyist-error reading (Keil-Delitzsch, Geisler-Howe), in which 35/36 in 2 Chr 15:19/16:1 are corruptions of an original 15/16; and (2) the divided-kingdom counting (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, endorsed by Thiele, p. 59), in which the figures count years from the schism rather than Asa's regnal years. The critical alternative (Klein, Japhet) treats the date as theological redaction rather than calendar or scribal slip. Each route concedes the surface text conflicts.

entries.question: Was Jehu the son or grandson of Nimshi?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 19:16 calls Jehu the son of Nimshi. 2 Kings 9:2 (and 9:14) calls him the son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi, making him Nimshi's grandson. The same person is given two different relationships to the same ancestor within the same narrative complex.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 19:16: "Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king." 2 Kings 9:2: "Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi." The simplest reading: one verse skips a generation.

The apologetic move, used by Archer and standard in Keil-Delitzsch, is that in Hebrew genealogy "son of" can mean "descendant of" — most famously in Matthew 1:1 where Jesus is called "the son of David, the son of Abraham" even though he is not literally David's or Abraham's son. So 1 Kings 19:16 just uses the looser sense, naming Jehu's more famous ancestor (Nimshi) without listing the immediate father (Jehoshaphat). This is a real lexical possibility — *ben* in Hebrew does have a wider range than English "son."

Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in their AB 11 *II Kings* (pp. 107-108) accept this as the simplest reading and treat the dual usage as a non-issue: 1 Kings 19:16 names the prominent patronymic, 2 Kings 9 spells out the full lineage. The contradiction dissolves at the lexical level if you grant the standard Hebrew sense of *ben*.

The weakness of this harmonization, raised by some critical scholars, is that 2 Kings 9 itself uses both formulas — Jehu is called "son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi" in 9:2 and 9:14, but "son of Nimshi" in 9:20. So the narrator alternates between the two forms within the same chapter. The harmonization that *ben* means "descendant of" works fine, but it concedes the texts are using imprecise language, which is the same kind of imprecision that elsewhere produces real chronological and genealogical headaches.

Verdict: this is one of the weaker SAB contradictions in the batch. The Hebrew lexical range really does cover the gap. But it's still worth listing because the imprecise use of *ben* is itself a feature of biblical historiography that produces actual contradictions in other passages (Matthean genealogy, anyone?). I'd lean toward keeping it on the list while flagging that the harmonization here is more solid than for the numerical entries. That is of course a subjective call on which contradictions count as real.

answers.answer: Jehu was the son of Nimshi.
answers.answer_explanation:
And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be
				          king. 1 Kings 19:16

answers.answer: Jehu was the grandson of Nimshi.
answers.answer_explanation:
And when thou commest thither, look out there Jehu the son
				          of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi and go in. 2 Kings 9:2

commentary_out.commentary:
The two patronymics are flatly different on the surface. 1 Kings 19:16 instructs Elijah: "Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel." 2 Kings 9:2 has the prophetic emissary seek out "Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi," and 9:14 repeats the three-tier line. Read woodenly in English, one verse makes Jehu Nimshi's son and the other makes him Nimshi's grandson.

The harmonization here is unusually robust and turns on Hebrew lexicography rather than special pleading. The noun *ben* ("son") regularly denotes any male descendant, not only a first-generation offspring. The Hebrew Bible uses it for grandsons (Genesis 29:5 calls Laban "son of Nahor" though he was Nahor's grandson via Bethuel), for remoter descendants ("sons of Israel" centuries after Jacob), and in the formula "son of David" applied to kings far down the Davidic line. The New Testament inherits the idiom: Matthew 1:1 names Jesus "the son of David, the son of Abraham," telescoping a thousand years. On this standard usage, 1 Kings 19:16 simply names Jehu by his more prominent ancestor, Nimshi, while 2 Kings 9 spells out the intervening father, Jehoshaphat. Naming a person by a famous grandfather rather than an obscure father was an ordinary ancient Near Eastern convention; "Jehu son of Nimshi" functions almost as a clan designation.

Cogan and Tadmor accept this as the obvious reading and treat the variation as a non-issue (AB 11, pp. 107-108): the short form is the recognized patronymic, the long form the complete pedigree. The contradiction dissolves at the lexical level once *ben* is granted its ordinary range — which it must be, since the same range is required to make sense of dozens of other genealogical notices.

The one genuinely interesting wrinkle is internal to 2 Kings 9 itself. The narrator uses the full three-generation form in 9:2 and 9:14 but reverts to the short "son of Nimshi" in 9:20, where the watchman recognizes Jehu's furious chariot-driving. The text thus alternates freely between the two formulas within a single chapter, which confirms that ancient writers did not regard the long and short forms as competing factual claims; they were interchangeable ways of identifying the same man. That very interchangeability is the point worth flagging: the loose use of *ben* that resolves this case cleanly is the same imprecision that, applied to figures and reign-lengths, produces irreducible contradictions elsewhere (the Asa-Baasha synchronism in 2 Chronicles 16, or the two divergent genealogies of Jesus in Matthew 1 and Luke 3). Here, however, no chronological or numerical claim hangs on the difference.

Sweeney (OTL, pp. 326-333) and Fritz (Continental Commentary, pp. 280-283) note the alternation without treating it as a real discrepancy, and even Archer's apologetic *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* (p. 213) reaches the same lexical conclusion that critical commentators do. When the harmonizing and critical camps converge on the same explanation, the case is weak as a contradiction.

Verdict: harmonizable, and among the weakest items in this batch. The semantic breadth of *ben* fully covers the gap, the same chapter uses both forms indifferently, and no datum of substance depends on whether Jehu is reckoned Nimshi's son or grandson. It earns a place on a contradiction list only as an illustration of the imprecise patronymic idiom that does real damage in genealogies and synchronisms elsewhere — not as a discrepancy in its own right.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Hebrew ben denotes any male descendant, not only a first-generation son; 1 Kings 19:16 names Jehu by his prominent grandfather Nimshi while 2 Kings 9:2,14 give the full lineage — and 2 Kings 9:20 itself uses the short form, showing the two patronymic styles were interchangeable.

entries.question: How old was Ahaziah when he began to reign?
entries.summary: 2 Kings 8:26 says Ahaziah was 22 when he began to reign. 2 Chronicles 22:2 says he was 42. Since his father Jehoram died at age 40 (2 Chronicles 21:20), the Chronicles figure makes Ahaziah older than his own father.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest numerical contradictions in the Hebrew Bible. 2 Kings 8:26 puts Ahaziah at 22. 2 Chronicles 22:2 puts him at 42. The arithmetic problem compounds: 2 Chronicles 21:5 and 21:20 say Jehoram was 32 when he began to reign and reigned 8 years, dying at 40. If his son Ahaziah was 42, the son outlived his father by two years before the father died. Mathematically impossible.

Apologists across the spectrum — Archer, Keil and Delitzsch, the older Geisler-Howe handbook — converge on the scribal-error explanation. The Hebrew numerical system, especially in pre-Masoretic transmission, used letter-based number representations that were easily corrupted. Archer argues 22 is original (2 Kings) and 42 is a transmission error (2 Chronicles). The LXX of 2 Chronicles 22:2 reads 22, supporting this. Syriac Peshitta and some Lucianic recensions also read 20 or 22.

This is one of those cases where critical scholarship and apologists actually agree on the diagnosis — scribal corruption — but disagree on what it implies. Ralph Klein in the Hermeneia 2 Chronicles volume, Sara Japhet in OTL, and Raymond Dillard in the WBC 2 Chronicles volume all acknowledge the textual error. The critical scholar's question is what this implies about inerrancy. If the autograph of 2 Chronicles 22:2 said 22 and a copyist wrote 42, the canonical text now contains an error. The Masoretic Text is what's canonical for Protestants. Anneli Aejmelaeus's work on the Old Greek of Samuel-Kings has documented dozens of similar numerical divergences between MT and LXX.

Verdict: a real, conceded contradiction in the received text. The harmonization is textual-critical — appeal to a corrected reading — and it works at the cost of acknowledging the received Masoretic text contains transmission errors. That's not a problem for critical scholarship. It is a problem for inerrancy as commonly defined.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest numerical contradictions in the Hebrew Bible, and unusually it is one where critical and conservative scholars agree on the mechanism while disagreeing about the stakes. 2 Kings 8:26 reports that Ahaziah was twenty-two (Hebrew *ben-'esrim u-shtayim shanah*) when he became king; 2 Chronicles 22:2 reports forty-two (*ben-'arba'im u-shtayim shanah*). The arithmetic problem is not subtle. 2 Chronicles 21:5 and 21:20 state that Ahaziah's father Jehoram became king at thirty-two and reigned eight years, dying at forty. If Ahaziah was forty-two at his own accession, which followed his father's death, he was two years older than his father — and would have been born two years before Jehoram himself was born. The figure is biologically impossible, not merely improbable.

The consensus diagnosis is scribal corruption. On the mechanism the cited commentators are more cautious than the older handbooks: numbers in the Masoretic Text and its known forebears are written out as words, and there is no manuscript evidence that the biblical text was ever transmitted using alphabetic numerals (the letter-value system — kaph = 20, mem = 40 — is attested on coins and in later usage, but as an explanation for these scribal slips it is a hypothesis, not a documented fact). The more defensible mechanism, and the one the critical commentaries actually argue, is corruption within the spelled-out number words themselves: "twenty" drifting to "forty" in copying. The versional evidence points to a figure in the low twenties as original. The Septuagint of 2 Chronicles 22:2 reads twenty (a minority of witnesses twenty-two), and the Syriac Peshitta likewise supports a figure in the low twenties; crucially, 2 Kings 8:26 reads twenty-two in both the MT and the LXX. The corruption is thus isolated to the Masoretic stream of Chronicles, exactly what a localized copying error predicts.

This is not an isolated phenomenon. The Hebrew text of Kings and Chronicles is riddled with parallel numerical divergences — the most famous being Jehoiachin's age at accession, eighteen in 2 Kings 24:8 but eight in 2 Chronicles 36:9, again an isolated single-stream error. Anneli Aejmelaeus and the broader school working on the Old Greek of Samuel–Kings have catalogued dozens of such cases, demonstrating that the numerical data in these books was among the least stable elements in transmission. Edwin Thiele, working from the conservative chronological side, reached the same conclusion about this verse: the forty-two is a copyist's slip.

Where the camps part ways is over implication. Gleason Archer, Keil and Delitzsch, and the Geisler–Howe handbook treat the correction as a vindication: the autograph said twenty-two, a scribe later wrote forty-two, and the "original" was therefore inerrant. Critical scholars — Ralph Klein in the Hermeneia Chronicles volume, Sara Japhet in the Old Testament Library, Raymond Dillard in the Word Biblical Commentary, Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in the Anchor Bible Kings volume — accept the textual-critical reconstruction but note its cost. Inerrancy as classically formulated by the Chicago Statement applies only to the non-existent autographs, never to any text actually possessed. For Protestant traditions that treat the Masoretic Text as canonical, the received text of 2 Chronicles 22:2 simply contains a false statement. The harmonization succeeds precisely by conceding that the canonical text errs.

Verdict: a genuine contradiction in the received text, resolved by appeal to a recoverable original reading — a textual-critical harmonization that works only at the price of admitting transmission error in the canonical Masoretic Chronicles.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Scribal corruption in the Masoretic stream of Chronicles: the original reading was a figure in the low twenties (2 Kings 8:26 reads twenty-two in both MT and LXX; the LXX of 2 Chronicles 22:2 reads twenty, with the Syriac supporting the lower figure), and a miscopying of the spelled-out number word produced forty-two. The tension dissolves at the level of the reconstructed original but persists in the received Masoretic text.

issues.problem: The Thiele citation gives 'rev. ed. (Kregel, 1983).' The 1983 revised/3rd edition of The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings was published by Zondervan (Grand Rapids); Kregel is the later reprint house that currently issues the title. Entry 276 in this same batch correctly cites the same work as 'Zondervan, 1983.' Minor intra-batch publisher inconsistency; Kregel is a genuine publisher of the work, so the citation is imprecise rather than fabricated.
